source.title: Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature-Specific Timescales in Language Model Representations
source.authors: Haoyang Luo; M. Zarlenga; M. Jamnik

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature analysis to language-model representations, testing whether selected sparse features have interpretable activations; it does not test the original toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports temporal persistence, reconstruction, probing, and monitoring results, but these do not measure overlapping, nearly orthogonal features or feature competition for dimensions. For V4, the directly relevant results are automated interpretability scores for selected SAE features. Subject-probing and prompt-injection results concern information in persistent states, not recovery of sparse features by a dictionary. The paper's other SAE baselines and cited findings are not treated as claim results.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAEs to build and evaluate a new temporal SAE variant (Persistent SAE). Its interpretability, reconstruction, probing and monitoring results measure how well that method and its baselines perform. It does not test whether superposition holds in toy models, whether capacity drives polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are canonical or one-dimensional. The feature-level autointerp scores it reports are method-performance metrics, not a test of whether LLMs contain sparse features.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also first show that standard SAE features already exhibit temporal persistence tied to document-level context. They then introduce Persistent SAEs, which learn per-feature timescales from reconstruction alone while keeping competitive reconstruction. Fast features are locally interpretable; slow features track subject and preserve prompt-injection signals with causal effect on a monitor.
record.recipe_differences: This paper trains temporal sparse autoencoders on language-model activations and measures interpretability and persistence; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method or measure its geometric predictions.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability is reported separately for high-λ and low-λ feature groups; no outcome sensitivity relevant to superposition geometry is tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard SAE features (BatchTopK, Matryoshka) on Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B show temporal persistence. Median R_j(τ) falls from 0.618 at lag 1 to 0.096 at lag 512 in natural documents, versus near zero in shuffled controls. Past activations also remove about 0.4–0.9% of reconstruction error at lag 1 (Sec. 3, App. D).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary features carry feature-specific temporal persistence across tokens that token-wise SAEs do not model.

fits_no_version.finding: Autointerp scores fall with learned timescale. For Persistent SAE, slow (high-λ) features score 0.84 on Pythia and 0.79 on Gemma, versus 0.93 and 0.89 for fast features (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How interpretable an SAE feature is under token-wise autointerp depends on the feature's temporal scale.

record.problems: The evidence relevant to V4 is limited to selected feature examples and automated interpretability scores, not a comprehensive measure of SAE recovery. The study does not test superposition geometry, feature overlap, capacity competition, feature completeness, or feature stability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows: the paper's other reported results concern temporal persistence, reconstruction, subject information, or prompt-injection monitoring, rather than a claim version's named behavior.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy networks, overlap or orthogonality geometry, sparsity transition, or regular geometry.
All of it: no capacity competition or dedicated-dimension analysis.
All of it: no alternative origins of polysemanticity.
Not tested as a claim. The paper reports no measure of features spread across neurons, and no dictionary-recovery test against ground truth.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicity of SAE features.
No comparison of one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Dictionary-wide mean autointerp scores for all SAEs: BatchTopK 0.91 (Pythia) and 0.87 (Gemma); Matryoshka, Temporal and Persistent around 0.85–0.89. These are method-performance numbers, but they are the only non-selected interpretability rates if anyone treats SAE recovery as V4 evidence.
missing.versions: V4 (only if treated as indirect evidence; not a test)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped. It rested only on curated qualitative examples (Tables 4–5) whose captions say all selected features score above 0.85, so those are selection values. The paper is an SAE-methods study, with no aim or result on superposition.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, feature overlap, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or neurons sharing features.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
Tests automated interpretability of selected SAE features, not whether features are distributed across neurons, or whether the learned dictionary recovers all model features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of superposed features.
